# Reducing gradient conflicts does not guarantee better multi-task behavior prediction

## TL;DR
On real Hillstrom visits and conversions, we compared separate training, equal-weight joint training, and a two-task PCGrad-style shared-layer projection. Eight models, 1,600 GPU updates, eight exact weight reloads, 56 independent checks. PCGrad reduced conversion Brier relative to joint training in both seeds, but still lost to a prior.

![Measured full holdout and evaluation pipeline](/assets/research/manager-multitask-pcgrad-2026-11-27.svg)

Figure: full frozen 12,808-case test split. Lower Brier is better; axes are separate.

| Arm | Visit Brier | Conversion Brier |
|---|---:|---:|
| Prior | 0.112230 | 0.007747 |
| Single-task 42 | 0.109208 | 0.007751 |
| Joint 42 | 0.109149 | 0.007782 |
| PCGrad 42 | 0.109159 | 0.007776 |
| Single-task 43 | 0.109241 | 0.007819 |
| Joint 43 | 0.109195 | 0.007853 |
| PCGrad 43 | 0.109191 | 0.007842 |

## Reproduction and limits
Verify source CSV hash and join the entire frozen split. Train 29,885; test 12,808; test positives 1,650 visits and 100 conversions. Train-only scaling, pretreatment covariates and randomized assignment. Shared 12→32→2 MLP, seeds 42/43, 200 updates per arm, MPS. This is a two-task implementation of the PCGrad principle, not a native TensorFlow or CAGrad reproduction.

Equal optimizer-step counts do not mean equal compute. The published split is not blind. These are factual behavior predictions, not causal effect estimates or LLM evaluations. No promotion.

[Code, evidence, and team follow-up](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/tree/main/files/research-artifacts/multitask-pcgrad-2026-11-27/)
